replying_to: Replying to VORTEX: Physics-Driven Data Augmentations for Consistency Training for Robust Accelerated MRI Reconstruction
display_title: Official Review of Paper4037 by Reviewer Pyg2

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed a method to reconstruct MRI images from undersampled MRI images without aliasing effect in order to reduce the duration of data acquisition during MRI scans. The experiment was done with a dataset that consists of fully-sampled examples in spatial-frequency domain and undersampled examples in the same domain. They suggested a semi-supervised training framework that conducts joint reconstruction for supervised scans, and instead of denoising, they proposed implementing a data augmentation pipeline for the unsupervised scans. The denoising objective from the Desai et al., 2021 is replaced with a data augmentation pipeline that enforces invariance to physics-driven augmentation and equivariance for image-based augmentation. Physics-driven data augmentation is done by adding noise and motion into k-space. In image-based data augmentation, they first transform the k-space fully-sampled data into image domain using coil sensitivity maps, then apply the image-based augmentation to both image and the sensitivity maps. Next, using the augmented image and transformed sensitivity maps, they run a forward model to generate the corresponding undersampled k-space measurement. Ablation studies are provided to compare pixel-based and latent-space consistency as well as data augmentation difficulty.
content.main_review:
Strength:
- Compared to MRAugment, the authors considered coil sensitivity maps in the image-based augmentation.
- The authors proposed a method to solve an important problem such as physics-based data augmentation to reconstruct MRI images from undersampled MRI image.
- Two ablation studies were preset; latent space vs pixel-level consistency and augmentation scheduling difficulty.

Weakness:
- The presented idea is not novel. Most of the operations seem to be done in the image domain with simple existing augmentation techniques, and the presented k-space is only used for the undersampling process.
- Details about the hyperparameter settings are missing. 
- Table 2: only one sota (MRAugment) is compared with the proposed method. The author should add more current works to prove their method.
- There is no Lsup in glossary (supplementary material)
- The presentation of figure 1 is very confusing. 
(1) It looks that only the undersampled data is undergoing data augmentation. But, in page 5, the last four lines, it states "Since the training data initially exists as fully-sampled k-space measurements, we first transform it into the image domain using coil sensitivity maps. We then apply a cascade of the image-based data augmentations to both the image and the sensitivity maps."  This is confusing.
(2) It might be useful to show the structure of f_theta(.,A). I guess f_theta first transforms y to image domain x and passes x through a u-net. But the figure looks that the f_theta is a single module to transform k-space to an image. Those two operations should be separated to avoid confusion.
(3) Augmentation seems to be done on images, but figure 1 looks that it is done on k-space.  In 4.1.2. the augmentation module seems to transform k-space into image domain and back to k-space after augmentation. This is very confusing.
(4) In the supervised part, the Omega seems to be multiplied twice, before the f and inside of the f. Is it correct?
- Figure 5 is mentioned in the paper but the figure is in the supplementary material.
content.summary_of_the_review:
- The idea of augmentation is well known and straightforward.
- Some parts of the papers are not clear and need improvements. E.g, figure 1 should be improved
- More previous work should be added for comparisons.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.

content.title: [1/2] Response to Reviewer Pyg2
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their comments. We respond to individual comments below. 

***“Most of the operations seem to be done in the image domain with simple existing augmentation techniques, and the presented k-space is only used for the undersampling process.”:*** We would like to clarify that VORTEX uses knowledge about the forward model of the MRI acquisition process to develop augmentations that are applied to the multi-coil k-space data. Hence our physics-based augmentations (noise and motion) are indeed conducted in the k-space. We, for the first time to the best of our knowledge, characterize the interface and study the interactions between physics-based MRI acquisition-motivated and image-based augmentations to 1) reduce data dependency and 2) increase robustness to clinically-relevant distribution shifts that are pervasive during MRI acquisition. We provide a detailed description of novel features and advantages of VORTEX in Appendix B and summarize these points in the general response.

**Hyperparameters and supplementary material:** We include a detailed description for all the relevant baselines that we compare to and their corresponding hyperparameters in Appendix D. We have included the definition of Lsup in Table 4 in the glossary, and Figure 5 is included in the Appendix to provide context for the augmentation scheduling, which is discussed in detail in the Appendix.

**Additional Comparisons to Existing Works:** We have implemented and compared VORTEX to another state-of-the-art baseline, namely self-supervised learning via data undersampling (SSDU) [1]. This method was originally proposed for fully unsupervised learning, in which all training scans are prospectively undersampled. We propose a trivial extension to adapt it for the semi-supervised setting. In cases of prospectively undersampled (unsupervised) data, the training protocol proposed in SSDU was used. Fully-sampled (supervised) data was retrospectively undersampled using the undersampling method and acceleration for the specified experiment. These simulated undersampled scans were used as inputs to the SSDU protocol. Specifically, we include SSDU in Table 2 and Table 9, and demonstrate that VORTEX outperforms SSDU by +8.5 SSIM for in distribution, +5.1 SSIM for the heavy motion, and +11.5 SSIM for the heavy noise settings (Table 2). We include statistical significance measures with respect to SSDU as well in Table 9 that shows SSIM improvements are significant (p<0.05). To the best of our knowledge, Noise2Recon, MRAugment, and SSDU are the closest approaches to our work all of which we compare to along with supervised and augmentation-based baselines. We include a detailed description for all the relevant baselines that we compare to and their corresponding hyperparameters in Appendix D.

**Clarification of Figure 1:** We thank the reviewer for their comments on Figure 1, we have revised it to be more interpretable. We respond to each of their questions in the following. 

(1) In MRAugment (i.e. supervised augmentations), the data augmentations are applied to the fully-sampled image prior to undersampling. However, in the consistency branch of VORTEX, only undersampled data are available. Thus, image augmentations in VORTEX are applied to the undersampled data. While composing augmentations, physics-driven acquisition-based augmentations (noise, motion) perturb the k-space first, and image-space augmentations (rotation, shearing, etc.) are applied after transforming the augmented k-space to image domain using the coil sensitivity maps. We have removed the term “fully-sampled” in Section 4.1.2 from the statement to avoid confusion: *“Since the training data initially exists as k-space measurements, we first transform it into the image domain using coil sensitivity maps.”*

(2) We separated transforming k-space to image space through the operation A^T, and the neural network f_theta that maps the zero-filled images (augmented or non-augmented) to the output model reconstructions. 

(3) Noise and motion augmentations are done directly on the undersampled k-space, and image-based augmentations are applied to both the image and the sensitivity maps after transforming to the image space. Consistency is enforced in the image space during consistency training. 

(4) Omega corresponds to the undersampling operation in the k-space, and it is only applied once.

content.title: [2/2] Response to Reviewer Pyg2
content.comment:
**New Dataset (fastMRI) Results:** We have included new experimental results for VORTEX and all other baselines on the fastMRI brain multi-coil dataset [2] in Table 10 to address reviewers’ comments around the effectiveness of our method for 2D vs. 3D MRI sequences. Specifically, we compare VORTEX to Supervised, SSDU, Aug (Motion), and MRAugment baselines for in distribution and OOD motion settings of different motion levels on the fastMRI multi-coil brain dataset. Data preparation and experimental details follow the description in Appendix D, and all experiments are conducted at 8x acceleration. We demonstrate that VORTEX has comparable performance to baselines for in distribution, and outperforms SSDU by +5.1 SSIM and +4.8 cPSNR, and MRAugment by +11.1 SSIM and +5.7 cPSNR on motion level alpha=0.6; SSDU by +9.8 SSIM and +5.8 cPSNR, and MRAugment by +14 SSIM and +6.5 cPSNR on motion level alpha=0.8; SSDU by +11 SSIM and +6.3 cPSNR, and MRAugment by +14.5 SSIM and +6.9 cPSNR on motion level alpha=1.0. This demonstrates that the effectiveness of VORTEX for both in distribution and OOD data generalizes to 2D MRI sequences which implies broader clinical utility.

**References:**

[1] Yaman, B., Hosseini, S. A. H., Moeller, S., Ellermann, J., Uğurbil, K., & Akçakaya, M. (2020). Self‐supervised learning of physics‐guided reconstruction neural networks without fully sampled reference data. Magnetic resonance in medicine, 84(6), 3172-3191.

[2] Zbontar, et al. “fastmri: An open dataset and benchmarks for accelerated MRI.” arXiv:1811.08839 (2018).

display_title: Official Review of Paper4037 by Reviewer BiXF

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors propose a domain knowledge injected data augmentation method for a semi-supervised deep learning-based MRI reconstruction from an undersampled frequency space. The goal is to both overcome the scarcity of ground-truth scans and improve the robustness against the distribution shifts in practical application. In this specific setup, they introduce transformations such as Gaussian noise and motion artifacts at the unsupervised part of the reconstruction network for consistency training. Experiments performed on knee MR images show considerable improvements in both in- and out-of-distribution scenarios compared to a few baselines.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
- The paper is well motivated that MRI reconstruction acceleration is necessary to be robust to distribution drifts when there’s not enough training labels.
- It’s beneficial to introduce domain knowledge such as signal-noise-ratio changes and motion artifacts into a deep learning network which is usually treated as a black box.
- The experimental results show significant reconstruction improvements meatured by SSIM and cPSNR.
	
Weaknesses:
- The proposed method performs consistency training but didn’t compared with any relevant papers in the literature.
- In this empirical paper, only a very small dataset (14 training, 2 validation, and 3 testing scans) is used to evaluate the proposed method, which is not convincing.
- The out-of-distribution samples are simulated by adding Gaussian noise and motion artifacts to good quality data. In the real scenario, distribution drifts could originate from a variety of factors such as acquisition protocol changes, scanner magnetic strength changes, and even modality changes.
- The paper uses 2D Unet to solve a 3D MRI reconstruction problem. A 3D Unet might be preferred.
- In the ablation study of varying the acceleration rate, the authors didn’t compare with the data augmentation baseline “MRAugment”.
- Although the proposed augmentation method shows better performance in SSIM, there’s marginal improvement in cPSNR.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper provides an empirical study on introducing a heuristic physical-inspired data augmentation method to a MRI reconstruction problem for robustness under testing distribution drifts with few supervised examples. However, larger-scale and diverse-samples are needed for method validation; real distribution drifts data are desired for the model robustness testing; a fair comparison with consistency training papers is preferred.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

content.title: [1/3] Response to Reviewer BiXF
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their time and their valuable suggestions. We have included our responses to each of the comments below:

**Comparison to relevant literature:** We thank the reviewer for their suggestion to compare to more existing works in the literature. To the best of our knowledge, Noise2Recon is the first and only work that does consistency training in the context of accelerated MRI reconstruction. However, Noise2Recon and other prior denoising work (e.g. RED [12]) have focused on the use of noise augmentations as a regularization method. Thus, in existing literature, there is a lack of understanding of how acquisition and image based augmentations can be leveraged simultaneously and whether regularization can be performed for inverse problems via denoising versus additional artifact types such as motion. We extend the semi-supervised consistency framework in Noise2Recon to handle both acquisition such as motion and image based perturbations in a way that is motivated by the physical model of the MRI acquisition process, and we compare to Noise2Recon in our experimental setup. (see Table 1 and Figure 3)

In addition to comparisons with state-of-the-art fully supervised, supervised + augmentation, MRAugment, and Noise2Recon baselines, we have included a comparison with another state-of-the-art self-supervised MRI reconstruction method, namely self-supervised learning via data undersampling (SSDU) [1] to Table 2, Table 9, and Table 10. SSDU partitions available k-space measurements into two disjoint sets. One of the sets is used for measurement consistency with the forward model, and the other set is used for defining the training loss in k-space. We provide details for how we generalized this method to a semi-supervised regime and include hyperparameters in Appendix D. VORTEX outperforms SSDU in both in-distribution by +1.5 cPSNR and +8.5 SSIM and out-of-distribution settings by +5.1 SSIM for heavy motion and by +1.4 cPSNR and +11.5 SSIM for heavy noise (Table 2). We include statistical significance measures with respect to SSDU as well in Table 9 that shows SSIM improvements are significant (p<0.05), and compare SSDU to other baselines and VORTEX on the fastMRI multi-coil brain dataset [4] in Table 10. These results suggest that VORTEX i) is more data-efficient in semi-supervised regimes and ii) is more robust to clinically-relevant distribution shifts.

**Dataset Size:** We thank the reviewer for raising this concern. We would like to clarify that one of the main motivations in our work is to perform well in the data-limited regimes as that is the prevalent setting in the clinic. We have also revised our experimental results to include 2D fastMRI brain multi-coil dataset [4] that consists of larger number of fully-sampled scans in Table 10. Specifically, we compare VORTEX to Supervised, SSDU, Aug (Motion), and MRAugment baselines for in distribution and OOD motion settings of different motion levels on the fastMRI multi-coil brain dataset. Data preparation and experimental details follow the description in Appendix D, and all experiments are conducted at 8x acceleration. We demonstrate that VORTEX has comparable performance to baselines for in distribution, and outperforms SSDU by +5.1 SSIM and +4.8 cPSNR, and MRAugment by +11.1 SSIM and +5.7 cPSNR on motion level alpha=0.6; SSDU by +9.8 SSIM and +5.8 cPSNR, and MRAugment by +14 SSIM and +6.5 cPSNR on motion level alpha=0.8; SSDU by +11 SSIM and +6.3 cPSNR, and MRAugment by +14.5 SSIM and +6.9 cPSNR on motion level alpha=1.0. This demonstrates that the effectiveness of VORTEX for both in distribution and OOD data generalizes to 2D MRI sequences which implies broader clinical utility.

We also would like to clarify that both of the datasets we used in our experiments (mridata multi-coil knee [11] and fastMRI multi-coil brain [4]) are both publicly available, and all the patient data they include are de-identified.

content.title: [2/3] Response to Reviewer BiXF
content.comment:
**Distribution Drifts:** We thank the reviewer for their comment on real distribution shifts. The reviewer raises a valid point that in MRI acquisition drifts might arise due to acquisition protocol changes, scanner magnetic strength changes, and even modality changes. However, it must be noted that curating datasets for evaluation of deep learning methods across such distribution shifts is a daunting task since raw k-space data is seldom saved for most MRI acquisitions. To the best of our knowledge there do not exist public datasets available at this time. On the other hand, the influence of signal-to-noise-ratio and motion drifts can be accurately modeled by information regarding the forward model of MRI [8,9]. Moreover, in MRI, field strength is directly proportional to signal-to-noise-ratio [10]. As a result, scanner magnetic strength changes can be modeled by signal-to-noise-ratio variations. Furthermore, acquisition changes such as varying number of averages, readout bandwidth, echo times, and resolution, all directly affect SNR. In this work, we further consider motion drifts, which are complex, patient-induced drifts that might occur with any acquisition protocol and any modality. As a result, for our initial work, we consider a setup where image acquisition is performed with a single acquisition protocol and single modality, and each anatomy (brain vs knee) in MRI is acquired with a different sequence variation representing a different acquisition type (2D vs 3D). We will consider modality, scanner, and acquisition protocol changes as part of our future work. 

**2D vs 3D Training:** We thank the reviewer for their comment. The mridata multi-coil knee dataset used in our experiments is acquired with a 3D fast-spin-echo (FSE) sequence where kx is the readout direction, i.e. fully-sampled acquisition is performed in the kx direction. As a result, undersampling is performed in the ky × kz direction, which makes the reconstruction problem separable across slices in the kx direction. Therefore, the training problem is commonly solved by reconstructing slices in the ky × kz direction separately. The 2D setup 1) avoids limiting network size due to memory constraints and 2) allows larger batch sizes, which have been shown to be effective for fully-convolutional networks like U-Net [2, 4]. Such approaches have shown to achieve state-of-the-art performance for MRI reconstruction [3, 4]. On the other hand, 3D networks are used for reconstructing spatiotemporal data where the problem cannot be solved using separate slices [5], and are undesirable due to increased computational and memory requirements [6]. 3D U-Net could easily be incorporated into our framework and we will seek to perform future experiments with it. However, the required time and memory requirements for training are infeasible in our existing computational infrastructure within the span of the rebuttal period.

**Acceleration rate results for MRAugment:** We thank the reviewer for this note. We have added experiments for MRAugment at both 12x and 16x accelerations to Table 8. We show that regardless of the acceleration, VORTEX outperforms all other baselines in both in-distribution and OOD settings. At 12x, VORTEX outperforms MRAugment by +0.2 cPSNR and +6 SSIM in in-distribution setting, +4.2 cPSNR and +6.9 SSIM for light motion artifacts, and +9.9 cPSNR and +20.9 SSIM for heavy motion artifacts.

**SSIM vs cPSNR:** We appreciate the reviewer’s note regarding differences in performance measured by SSIM and cPSNR. While cPSNR has been used to quantify image quality, it often prioritizes low frequency information which is easier to recover during MRI reconstruction [4]. On the other hand, SSIM has shown more promise for discriminating images based on higher frequency information and has shown higher concordance with visual radiologist image quality scores [7]. We include this sentence and a corresponding reference in Section 5.1 to qualify the importance of SSIM:

“SSIM has shown to be a more clinically-preferred metric to cPSNR for quantifying perceptual quality of MRI reconstructions (Knoll et al., 2020).”

As the reviewer mentioned, while our method showed improvement in SSIM and cPSNR, the performance difference measured for SSIM was larger than the performance difference measured for cPSNR. We also included statistical significance results based on SSIM for both Table 1 and Table 2. Since our method aims to recover global structural changes such as motion, an SSIM improvement indicates that clinically relevant high frequency information that was altered by such structural changes can be recovered more effectively by our method. Although the balance between recovering high-frequency vs. low-frequency information can be altered by hyperparameters such as regularization strength, it is desirable for VORTEX to perform more favorably in recovering clinically relevant high frequency information, and thus remove global structural artifacts.

content.summary_of_the_paper: [Summary] This work addresses the problem of data augmentation for MRI reconstruction, where the image reconstruction depends on the quality of the acquired spatial-frequency space. This motivates a scheme that is based on  physics-driven and image-based augmentations. The core idea of the paper is such a combination of types of augmenters. The authors build upon the semi-supervised framework of that (Desai et al, 2021). The experimental results show potentials in the results wrt existing schemes.
content.main_review:
-- Whilst the idea of incorporating   physics-driven and image-based augmentations, for MRI reconstruction, is appealing. A major  factor that somehow turns down the paper is the clear level of technical contribution. Firstly, the authors general framework builds strongly on that (Desai et al, 2021) which differs from the incorporation of  the  physics-driven and image-based augmentations. (Desai et al, 2021) already consider ODD shifts from the variation on SNR in the acquisitions, authors extend such scheme by including affine motion as another factor of degradation ( different type of motion based augmentation has been already explored in other works such as in [*]). Therefore, the technical contribution is appreciated as incremental and mainly being an empirical paper (no theoretical findings are provided). Authors need to strengthen the difference in findings from other works, as the major message that  physics-aware and image-based augmentations are key in performance has been already reported in (Desai et al, 2021) and (Fabian et al., 2021). 


[*] Shaw, Richard, et al. "MRI k-space motion artefact augmentation: model robustness and task-specific uncertainty." International Conference on Medical Imaging with Deep Learning, 2018


-- There is a lack of motivation and discussion on why to limit the framework to 2D Poission Disc sampling pattern. Is there any reason?  What about other typical sampling patterns -- for example spiral sampling? Whilst I agree that authors cover one relevant one, other patterns such as spiral sampling are not only interesting at the clinical level but also at the technical level. For example, dealing with the non-uniformly acquired data whilst having some advantages over the selected such as less degradation in the image quality. Authors should argue this limitation.

-- Differences with MRAugment. Authors stated “In contrast to MRAugment, we incorporate MRI physics into the augmentations pipeline by embedding MRI coil sensitivity” and “using image-based data augmentation schemes (Fabian et al., 2021)”. Such arguments are unclear. Firstly, the authors of MRAugment main motivation is taking into account the physics behind the MRI acquisition, and also consider coil sensitivities. Also, the principles of the scheduling seems to be motivated by such work. Can the authors strengthen  their main advantages over MRAugment?

-- [Experimental Results] The experimental setting has merit. It would be beneficial to further support the numerical advantages of the authors scheme with a statistical test. 

--[Other] There are some parts in the description that seem not to have a purpose throughout the paper. For example subsection 3.2 authors define Equivariance and Invariance. However, such concepts are barely linked in the main paper or why such known concepts need a full subsection. 


------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
POST-REBUTTAL

After reading carefully the rebuttal, the authors addressed my concerns and I further agree with the value of the paper. My thoughts are  alined by the general positive comments of the majority of the other reviewers. 
The authors included, in the updated version, all clarifications including the statistical tests requested and further discussion on my questions. Overall, I’m more positive about this paper than before and this is therefore reflected in the final suggested score.
content.summary_of_the_review: This is a lower borderline paper. The author need to further support the main technical advantages of their proposed scheme wrt of existing works (see previous point), as currently the paper is appreciated with an incremental contribution.  Moreover, the strong claims would be better supported with a set of statistical tests.   (see Post-rebuttal comments).

content.title: [1/4] Response to Reviewer ZVy8
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their time and their valuable suggestions. We have included clarifications to each of the comments below.

### Technical Contributions
We thank the reviewer for raising this point. VORTEX builds upon valuable existing work in image-based augmentations (MRAugment, Fabian et al.) and consistency training for OOD mitigation (Noise2Recon, Desai et al.).

However, there are some important nuanced differences between these works. MRAugment focuses on image-based augmentations (rotation, scale, shear, etc.) and their utility in a fully supervised training regime. Noise2Recon uses *noise augmentations* as a regularization method in a semi-supervised consistency framework, but does not consider other relevant MRI acquisition augmentations. Thus, in existing literature, there is a lack of understanding of how acquisition and image based augmentations can be leveraged simultaneously and whether regularization can be performed for inverse problems via additional artifact correction tasks beyond denoising (e.g. motion correction).

In this work, we characterize the interface between physics-based MRI acquisition-motivated and image-based augmentations to 1) reduce data dependency and 2) increase robustness to clinically-relevant distribution shifts that are pervasive during MRI acquisition. We extend the semi-supervised consistency framework in Noise2Recon to handle both acquisition and image-based perturbations in a way that is motivated by the physics-driven forward model of MRI acquisition.

To ensure that we are inclusive of a broader family of acquisition-based perturbations than was available in Noise2Recon, we propose extending the semi-supervised consistency framework proposed to handle motion, a common artifact in MRI. We exhaustively study the interaction between acquisition based and image based augmentations in both fully supervised training with augmentations and semi-supervised training with the proposed consistency framework. We make a distinction between sets of data augmentations that we would like to be invariant vs. equivariant to based on the desired behavior at inference time. 

We have added an in-depth discussion of differences from MRAugment and Noise2Recon in Appendix B. 

We have also added the references for motion augmentations suggested by the reviewer into the related work. However, we note that such augmentations proposed in these works were not designed for a reconstruction setting, but rather a segmentation setting, where motion was applied to magnitude images. Since motion in MRI leads to k-space phase shifts, augmentations must be performed in the complex domain. We formulate the motion augmentation to transform complex images.

### 2D Poisson Disc Sampling
We thank the reviewer for this note. While non-Cartesian sampling trajectories like spiral are an active area of research, they are often susceptible to eddy current and gradient timing artifacts when deployed prospectively. As such, the vast majority of research and clinical scans are acquired with Cartesian sampling. The 2D Poisson Disc sampling method was selected 1) to ensure that the sampling pattern was motivated by the constraints and practical feasibility of acquiring the types of scans available in this dataset and 2) to study the utility of cutting-edge compressed-sensing undersampling patterns among machine-learning reconstruction methods.

We have also updated our work to include results using the fastMRI multi-coil brain dataset in Table 10 to show the generalizability of our method to different acquisition types (2D vs 3D) and anatomy (brain vs knee). Results are discussed in detail in General Response, and details for these experiments are provided in Appendix F.

We have added this motivation to Appendix C.1 and have added the suggestion of exploring other sampling trajectories to our plans for future work:
- Appendix C.1: Scans for training and evaluation were undersampled using 2D Poisson Disc undersampling, a compressed sensing-motivated pattern for 3D Cartesian imaging.
- Conclusion: In future work, we plan to extend our VORTEX physics-driven augmentations to additional OOD MRI artifacts and non-Cartesian undersampling patterns to work towards building robust DL-based MR reconstruction models that can be safely deployed in clinics.

content.title: [2/4] Response to Reviewer ZVy8
content.comment:
### Differences with MRAugment
We thank the reviewer for their thorough review of both VORTEX and MRAugment. We provide a summary of the distinctions between our method and MRAugment below. We have also added these distinctions to Appendix B.1.

**Relaxing the assumption of preserved noise statistics:** In their work, the authors of MRAugment argue that augmentations must preserve noise statistics of the data: *“It is important that the augmentation function preserves the noise distribution of training images as much as possible. Indeed, a large mismatch between training and test noise distribution leads to poor generalization”* (MRAugment, Section 3.1). 

We verify this assumption is relevant to standard augmentations in supervised training where we see degraded performance among in-distribution scans (Table 1).

However, in the VORTEX framework, this assumption can be relaxed, likely due to the use of consistency training. We empirically demonstrate that VORTEX can use augmentations that do not preserve distributional noise (e.g. noise and motion augmentations) and can achieve state-of-the-art performance among in-distribution scans even in data-limited regimes (Table 2). We believe that relaxing this assumption is critical for leveraging a generalized family of augmentations in practical applications without carefully preserving the noise distribution of the training and testing data. We will conduct more theory-oriented work in the future about why consistency training is helpful based on this observation.

We provide a detailed discussion about this property in Appendix B.1. We also add the paragraph below to Section 5.3: VORTEX vs Baselines:

*“The substantial performance gain with VORTEX in both in-distribution and OOD settings may suggest that the consistency framework is amenable to both image-based and acquisition-based augmentations. While conventional supervised training requires that all augmentations preserve the noise statistics of the training data, consistency training can relax this constraint and allow for the use of acquisition-based augmentations (see Appendix B.1).”*

**Image-based vs acquisition-based augmentations:** While MRAugment does introduce augmentations that respect the multi-coil MRI acquisition setup, referred to as *physics-driven*, the augmentations introduced are solely in the image domain. VORTEX pairs these image-level augmentations with augmentations that are motivated by the physics of the MRI acquisition.

content.title: [3/4] Response to Reviewer ZVy8
content.comment:
### Differences with MRAugment (ctd.)

**Coil sensitivities - Learned vs Precomputed:** MRAugment utilizes the E2E-VarNet [6], which *learns* to jointly estimate coil sensitivities and reconstruct images. Thus, the process of sensitivity map estimation is optimized in the presence of augmentations. Because the learning process includes optimization of sensitivity maps, reported experiments in MRAugment need not consider the impact of precomputed sensitivity maps, which are fixed (i.e. not optimized). In practice, precomputing coil sensitivities is feasible and routine with sensitivity map estimation methods such as ESPiRIT and JSENSE [1,2]. The use of precomputed sensitivity maps also allows us to leverage multi-coil datasets where the number of coils are not constant across different scans - an important consideration when patients with heterogeneous anatomies are being imaged, as has been demonstrated in newer MRI datasets [4].

While MRAugment does acknowledge the use of precomputed sensitivity maps (MRAugment, Eq. 3.3), the formulation assumes that these sensitivity maps are fixed in the presence of image-based augmentations. However, based on physical models, image-based augmentations that are designed to emulate shifts in the imaging target also impact the coil geometry and sensitivity maps that are estimated. For example, bulk affine movement (rotation, translation, etc) of the anatomical target would result in the coil shifting along the direction of motion. Scaling (zoom-in/zoom-out) the image represents a changing field of view and changing scan resolution, which would result in similar scaling of coil sensitivities. Because sensitivity maps are directly estimated from the image, image-based augmentations, which perturb the underlying image, can warp the precomputed sensitivity maps.

Motivated by the physics of the coil setup, we propose applying image-based augmentations to *both* the image and the sensitivity maps.

We thank the reviewer for mentioning that this distinction can be unclear. We have clarified this distinction in Appendix B.1. We have also rephrased the sentence mentioned by the reviewer to emphasize that VORTEX does not require that augmentations preserve noise statistics of the training data.

*“Additionally while MRAugment is constrained to image augmentations to preserve noise statistics in the training data, we demonstrate that VORTEX can relax this constraint and operate on a broad family of augmentations, including acquisition-based augmentations, which inherently change noise statistics of the training data.”*

**Augmentation Scheduling - Probability vs Difficulty:** MRAugment proposed scheduling the probability of applying an augmentation. In VORTEX, we propose a curriculum learning strategy of scheduling the *difficulty* of the augmentation.

The distinction originates from the motivation for the different scheduling approaches. MRAugment notes that “*in initial stages of training no augmentation is needed*” and that augmentations are introduced to reduce overfitting (MRAugment, Section 3.3). Thus, probability scheduling reduces the likelihood of seeing augmented data in early training stages.

In VORTEX, we are interested in *building robustness to OOD perturbations*, where the *extent* (and, more generally, difficulty) of these perturbations will be unknown at test time. Thus, the model must learn to jointly optimize for both in-distribution (default training data) and OOD (perturbation-corrupt data) examples. Intuitively, we need to design an augmentation scheduling scheme that will allow the model to gradually learn to generalize to higher extents (more difficult) perturbations over time while still ensuring the model “sees” examples from both distributions for joint optimization. 

Scheduling difficulty may also have the added benefit of being more intuitive for evaluating network performance. In cases where augmentation difficulty may be closely linked to the augmentation extent, which is often the case with acquisition-based artifacts (e.g. more noise/motion -> more corrupt images -> harder image recovery), scheduling these parameters may provide a more intuitive characterization of the difficulty of the task.

content.title: [4/4] Response to Reviewer ZVy8
content.comment:
### Statistical significance of experimental results
We thank the reviewer for this note. We have added statistical significance measures for slice-wise metrics to Table 9 and explanation to Appendix F. We demonstrate that VORTEX has significantly higher SSIM (p<0.05) on the mridata knee dataset compared to supervised, augmentation-based, a newly implemented self-supervised learning technique SSDU [5], and MRAugment in both in-distribution and OOD settings. VORTEX’s performance is particularly strong in the OOD settings, leading to an improvement of +12.3 SSIM over MRAugment and +6.4 SSIM over SSDU for the heavy motion case; and an improvement of +9.5 SSIM over MRAugment and +13 SSIM over SSDU for the heavy noise case. This indicates that VORTEX has higher fidelity in recovering image structure even in OOD settings where perturbations can result in a considerable degradation in SSIM. 

### Equivariance and Invariance
We appreciate the reviewer’s request to clarify the importance of the terms *equivariance* and *invariance*.

VORTEX proposes a unified framework for leveraging both image-based and acquisition-based augmentations to “encourage” different properties when training the model (e.g. invariance to motion artifacts). Specifically, these augmentations can be defined by the relationship between the augmented input and the expected output of the model.

The terms equivariance and invariance are frequently used in ML and signal processing literature for defining this relationship [3]. We hope that using standardized terms for characterizing the behavior of different augmentations can help clarify the motivation behind our method.

We thank the reviewer for noting the disconnect between the relevance of Section 3.2 and the method. We have added the following sentence at the end of the section to direct readers to a more detailed discussion in Appendix B regarding the relevance of these terms :

“Details on how these definitions motivate the structure of augmentation(s) in VORTEX are provided in Appendix B.”

[2] Ying, L., & Sheng, J. (2007). Joint image reconstruction and sensitivity estimation in SENSE (JSENSE). Magnetic Resonance in Medicine: An Official Journal of the International Society for Magnetic Resonance in Medicine, 57(6), 1196-1202.

[3] Goodfellow, I., Bengio, Y., & Courville, A. (2016). Deep learning. MIT press.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors proposed VORTEX, a consistency training framework for data augmentation pipeline which is for the accelerated MRI reconstruction. VORTEX augments the data in two different ways: physics-driven augmentation for noise and motion and image-based augmentation by flipping, scaling, rotation, translation, shearing, etc,  which enforces invariance and equivariance, retrospectively.
The proposed augmentation framework improves data-efficiency and robustness to clinically relevant distribution drifts. 
The data augmentation methods are very important especially in medical field and the proposed method shows a superior MR reconsruction results compared to the other MR augmentation methods.
content.main_review:
*Strengths
- They defined the physics-driven noise by adding noise in k-space domain (g_N) & adding different random phase noise on odd/even k-spaces which simulates the patients motion (g_M). Compared to the natural image data augmentation, physics-driven approaches are the necessary processing for the MR reconstruction. 
- The reconstruction performance of VORTEX are superior in SSIM and cPSNR metric compared to the other conventional augmentation methods.
*weaknesses
- They called 'the reconstruction of the augmented input is mapped to non-augmented ground-truth' as 'invariance', but it is conventional approaches for the noise augmentation. Adding different noise on even/odd k-space is somewhat different for the conventional method. But, I couldn't find enough originality for the concept.

- The consistency training for MR data augmentation was already tried in [Noise2Recon: A Semi-Supervised Framework for Joint MRI Reconstruction and Denoising, arXiv 2021] & [Enhancing MR Image Segmentation with Realistic Adversarial Data Augmentation, arXiv 2021]. Please, cite this paper as reference.

- (Figure 3. the result of MRAugment): It is reasonable the results of heavy motion is poor. However, I think the reconstruction performance of MRAgument for heavy noise should be better than the displayed results. According to the supplementary material, I think the author used default parameter setting of MRAugment for the comparison. Please, specify the hyper-parameters of the augmentation methods for the comparison (in the supplementary material). It helps the reader can judge the fairness of the comparison.

- (Table.6) The 3 methods were trained by same number of epochs (=200). The results of VORTEX seems saturated (VORTEX results of 50%=results of 100%), but the Supervised and Aug(Motion) seems to has some room for improvement (results of 50%<results of 100%). The author might say 'the proposed method converged faster and better'. However, the proposed method uses both supervised and consistency paths and it results to the 3 times of network inferences and 3 times of backpropagation (1 for supervised & 2 for consistency, refer to Figure.1). The training time in the unit of time(or computational unit) might helpful to the user. Or the other comparative results should be converged to some optima even it takes 3 times more epochs than the training of VORTEX.

- I'm wondering the performance of the proposed method on 2D k-space sampling. In clinic, not only 3D MRI but also 2D MRI are both  widely used and needed to be accelerated because of respiration/motion/cardiac motion issues. 

- The author mentions that their results are superior because the the comparative reconstructions are noisy/blurry and show some artifacts. However, some radiologist might score better on the comparative one to examine the anatomy/lesion even it has heavy noise. The blind examination by the radiologist might be helpful as further work.

content.title: [1/2] Response to Reviewer DjEt
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their time and helpful comments. We clarify our technical contributions in comparison to existing works in General Response, and we respond to each of the comments below.

**Noise and motion augmentations:** In classification (image-to-label) problems, data augmentations are designed such that the labels stay invariant with respect to the augmentations. However, the accelerated MR reconstruction task at hand is an image-to-image problem, hence, data augmentations need to transform the target images and their corresponding k-space and coil sensitivity measurements. As such, we make a distinction between sets of data augmentations that we would like to be invariant vs. equivariant to based on the desired behavior at inference time.

As an example, we would like the output reconstruction to be invariant to the input noise in the undersampled scan. Meanwhile, if the input undersampled scan is rotated by 90 degrees, we also want the output reconstruction to be rotated by 90 degrees (rotation equivariance). We hope that clarifies why we associate the noise augmentation with “invariance” in this context. We model one-dimensional translational motion artifacts using random phase errors that alter odd and even lines of k-space separately. This is because many MRI acquisitions perform “multi-shot” imaging where k-space is acquired in an interleaved manner [1]. This augmentation method is not conventional outside of MRI reconstruction, however, and directly takes MRI physics and practical data acquisition techniques into account. It allows modifying both 2D and 3D MRI sequences that are commonly used in the clinic.

**Comparison with MRAugment:** We have included exact hyperparameters used for MRAugment in Table 5 and other augmentation methods in the Appendix D. Regarding the comment “However, I think the reconstruction performance of MRAugment for heavy noise should be better than the displayed results.”, MRAugment states that augmentations must preserve noise statistics of the acquired data: “It is important that the augmentation function preserves the noise distribution of training images as much as possible. Indeed, a large mismatch between training and test noise distribution leads to poor generalization” (MRAugment, Section 3.1). Considering we are evaluating all the methods in a setting where there is a fundamental noise distribution shift, MRAugment has poor generalization as the MRAugment authors pointed out in their paper. Furthermore, to encourage reproducibility for such questions, we have included all our code as supplementary material.

**Training length:** We revised our paper to include 200% and 300% training length times for Supervised, MRAugment, and Aug (Motion) baselines along with our method VORTEX in Table 7, as suggested by the reviewer. We demonstrate that VORTEX considerably outperforms all the baselines in the OOD settings; leading to +0.5 cPSNR over Aug (Motion), +2.3 cPSNR over MRAugment, +1.8 cPSNR over Supervised in Motion (light) setting, and +0.9 cPSNR over Aug (Motion), +8.0 cPSNR over MRAugment, +5.4 cPSNR over Supervised in Motion (heavy) setting at 300% training length. We also show that cPSNR of all methods are comparable at 300% for in distribution data, and that VORTEX achieves higher SSIM (Table 1, Table 2) and significantly higher per-slice SSIM (Table 9, p<0.05) compared to all baselines. We also would like to clarify that the gradient is not propagated through the pseudo-labels generated from non-augmented examples following the other semi-supervised consistency training frameworks [2], so each example is only seen once during training in a single epoch (one backpropagation per example per epoch).

replying_to: Replying to [1/2] Response to Reviewer DjEt

content.title: [2/2] Response to Reviewer DjEt
content.comment:
**2D vs. 3D MRI:** We would like to clarify that we demonstrated results on mridata that consists of 3D knee MRI scans and conducted 2D Poisson variable density k-space sampling. We have added new experimental results for VORTEX and all other baselines on the fastMRI brain multi-coil dataset [3] that consists of 2D MRI data that use 1D random undersampling. Specifically, in Table 10, we compare VORTEX to Supervised, SSDU, Aug (Motion), and MRAugment baselines for in distribution and OOD motion settings at different motion levels on the fastMRI multi-coil brain dataset. Data preparation and experimental details follow the description in Appendix D, and all experiments are conducted at 8x acceleration. We demonstrate that VORTEX has comparable performance to baselines for in distribution, and outperforms SSDU by +5.1 SSIM and +4.8 cPSNR, and MRAugment by +11.1 SSIM and +5.7 cPSNR on motion level alpha=0.6; SSDU by +9.8 SSIM and +5.8 cPSNR, and MRAugment by +14 SSIM and +6.5 cPSNR on motion level alpha=0.8; SSDU by +11 SSIM and +6.3 cPSNR, and MRAugment by +14.5 SSIM and +6.9 cPSNR on motion level alpha=1.0. This demonstrates that the effectiveness of VORTEX for both in distribution and OOD data generalizes to 2D MRI sequences which implies broader clinical utility. The 2D and 3D MRI scan types in these datasets exemplify a majority of clinically-utilized scans. Thus, results on these datasets may be relevant indicators for practical utility of our method.

**Other:** We thank the reviewer for their suggestion to do a radiologist reader study, and will certainly conduct this as part of our future work. We have revised our paper to cite “Enhancing MR Image Segmentation with Realistic Adversarial Data Augmentation, arXiv 2021” that proposes an adversarial data augmentation model which gets jointly optimized with a segmentation network.

**References:**

[1] Anderson, A.W., & Gore, J.C. (1994). Analysis and correction of motion artifacts in diffusion weighted imaging. Magnetic Resonance in Medicine, 32.

[2] Xie, Q., Dai, Z., Hovy, E.H., Luong, M., & Le, Q.V. (2020). Unsupervised Data Augmentation for Consistency Training. NeurIPS.

content.title: [1/2] General Response
content.comment:
We thank all the reviewers for their valuable time and insightful feedback. We are encouraged that R1 & R3 found our results significant, noting that “data augmentation methods are very important” and that “experimental results show significant reconstruction improvements” for addressing “distribution shifts in practical application(s)”. 

R1 & R2 expressed our experimental results show potential compared to existing methods; R4 expressed the importance of the problem we are tackling and considered our ablations and coil sensitivity map integration to image-based augmentations strong; and R3 found our work well-motivated as it enables robustness to distribution drifts despite limited training labels and stated that it is beneficial to introduce domain knowledge into a deep learning network that is often treated as a black box. We address the concerns that are shared across several reviewers below. Changes to the manuscript are indicated in blue font in the new submission.

**Significance of the Experimental Results:** We have added statistical significance measures for slice-wise metrics to Table 9 and explanation of these results to Appendix F. We demonstrate that VORTEX has significantly higher SSIM (p<0.05) on the mridata knee dataset compared to supervised methods, augmentation-based methods, a newly implemented self-supervised learning technique SSDU [1], and MRAugment in both in-distribution and OOD settings. VORTEX’s performance is particularly strong in the OOD settings, leading to an improvement of +12.3 SSIM over MRAugment and +6.4 SSIM over SSDU for the heavy motion case; and an improvement of +9.5 SSIM over MRAugment and +13 SSIM over SSDU for the heavy noise case. This indicates that VORTEX has higher fidelity in recovering image structure even in OOD settings where perturbations can result in a considerable degradation in SSIM. 

**New Comparisons to Existing Works:** We have implemented and compared VORTEX to another state-of-the-art baseline, namely self-supervised learning via data undersampling (SSDU). This method was originally proposed for fully unsupervised learning, in which all training scans are prospectively undersampled. We propose a trivial extension to adapt it for the semi-supervised setting. In cases of prospectively undersampled (unsupervised) data, the training protocol proposed in SSDU was used. Fully-sampled (supervised) data was retrospectively undersampled using the undersampling method and acceleration for the specified experiment. These simulated undersampled scans were used as inputs to the SSDU protocol. Specifically, we include SSDU in Table 2, Table 9, and Table 10, and demonstrate that VORTEX outperforms SSDU by +8.5 SSIM for in distribution, +5.1 SSIM for the heavy motion, and +11.5 SSIM for the heavy noise settings (Table 2). We include statistical significance measures with respect to SSDU as well in Table 9 that shows SSIM improvements are significant (p<0.05), and compare SSDU to other baselines and VORTEX on the fastMRI multi-coil brain dataset [2] in Table 10. To the best of our knowledge, Noise2Recon, MRAugment, and SSDU are the closest approaches to our work all of which are used as baselines along with supervised and augmentation-based methods. We include a detailed description for all the relevant baselines that we compare to and their corresponding hyperparameters in Appendix D.

**New Dataset (fastMRI) Results:** We have included new experimental results for VORTEX and all other baselines on the fastMRI brain multi-coil dataset [2] in Table 10 to address reviewers’ comments around the effectiveness of our method for 2D vs. 3D MRI sequences. Specifically, we compare VORTEX to Supervised, SSDU, Aug (Motion), and MRAugment baselines for in distribution and OOD motion settings of different motion levels on the fastMRI multi-coil brain dataset. Data preparation and experimental details follow the description in Appendix D, and all experiments are conducted at 8x acceleration. We demonstrate that VORTEX has comparable performance to baselines for in distribution, and outperforms SSDU by +5.1 SSIM and +4.8 cPSNR, and MRAugment by +11.1 SSIM and +5.7 cPSNR on motion level alpha=0.6; SSDU by +9.8 SSIM and +5.8 cPSNR, and MRAugment by +14 SSIM and +6.5 cPSNR on motion level alpha=0.8; SSDU by +11 SSIM and +6.3 cPSNR, and MRAugment by +14.5 SSIM and +6.9 cPSNR on motion level alpha=1.0. This demonstrates that the effectiveness of VORTEX for both in distribution and OOD data generalizes to 2D MRI sequences which implies broader clinical utility.

content.title: [2/2] General Response
content.comment:
**Additional Ablations:** (i) We have revised our paper to include 200% and 300% training length times for Supervised, MRAugment, and Aug (Motion) baselines along with our method VORTEX in Table 7. We demonstrate that VORTEX considerably outperforms all the baselines in the OOD settings; leading to +0.5 cPSNR over Aug (Motion), +2.3 cPSNR over MRAugment, +1.8 cPSNR over Supervised in Motion (light) setting, and +0.9 cPSNR over Aug (Motion), +8.0 cPSNR over MRAugment, +5.4 cPSNR over Supervised in Motion (heavy) setting at 300% training length. We also show that cPSNR of all methods are comparable at 300% for in distribution data, and that VORTEX achieves higher SSIM (Table 1, Table 2) and significantly higher per-slice SSIM (Table 9, p<0.05) compared to all baselines. (ii) We have added experiments for MRAugment at both 12x and 16x accelerations to Table 8. We show that regardless of the acceleration, VORTEX outperforms all other baselines in both in-distribution and OOD settings. At 12x, VORTEX outperforms MRAugment by +0.2 cPSNR and +6 SSIM in in-distribution setting, +4.2 cPSNR and +6.9 SSIM for light motion artifacts, and +9.9 cPSNR and +20.9 SSIM for heavy motion artifacts.

**Clarification of Technical Contributions:** We acknowledge that VORTEX builds upon valuable existing work in image-based augmentations (MRAugment, Fabian et al., 2021) and consistency training for OOD mitigation (Noise2Recon, Desai et al., 2021). However, there are several important differences between these works. MRAugment focuses on image-based augmentations (rotation, scale, shear, etc.) and their utility in a fully supervised training regime. Noise2Recon and other prior denoising work (e.g. RED [3]) have focused on the use of noise augmentations as a regularization method. Thus, in existing literature, there is a lack of understanding of how acquisition and image based augmentations can be leveraged simultaneously and whether regularization can be performed for inverse problems via denoising versus additional artifact types such as motion. In this work, we, for the first time to the best of our knowledge, characterize the interface between physics-based MRI acquisition-motivated and image-based augmentations to 1) reduce data dependency and 2) increase robustness to clinically-relevant distribution shifts that are pervasive during MRI acquisition. We extend the semi-supervised consistency framework in Noise2Recon to handle both acquisition and image based perturbations in a way that is motivated by the physical model of the MRI acquisition process. To ensure that we are inclusive of a broader family of acquisition-based perturbations than was available in Noise2Recon, we propose extending the semi-supervised consistency framework proposed to handle motion - one of the most common perturbations in MRI. We exhaustively study the interaction between physics/acquisition based and image based augmentations in both fully supervised training with augmentations and semi-supervised training with the proposed consistency framework. We make a distinction between sets of data augmentations that we would like to be invariant vs. equivariant to based on the desired behavior at inference time. We have added an in-depth discussion of differences from Noise2Recon and MRAugment in Appendix B.

**References:**

[1] Yaman, B., Hosseini, S. A. H., Moeller, S., Ellermann, J., Uğurbil, K., & Akçakaya, M. (2020). Self‐supervised learning of physics‐guided reconstruction neural networks without fully sampled reference data. Magnetic resonance in medicine, 84(6), 3172-3191.

[2] Zbontar, et al. “fastmri: An open dataset and benchmarks for accelerated MRI.” arXiv:1811.08839 (2018). 

[3] Romano, Y., Elad, M., & Milanfar, P. (2017). The little engine that could: Regularization by denoising (RED). SIAM Journal on Imaging Sciences, 10(4), 1804-1844.
